verdicts.reasoning: Same diagnosis, verified in sources.py:_get_json (key includes api_key from papers/paper_count, write_text, only 200 cached, Redis copy with full TTL) and core/redis.py (failure memoised forever, reset_redis unused). A is the base because its hash input equals today's string when no credential is set (zero-migration), its single-flight lock is sized per HTTP call (each _get_json call is one key) with blocking_timeout > fetch time, and it adds a warm/founder caller class to _over_budget. B's lock reasons about three calls per key (papers makes three different keys, so this is a misreading) and its blocking_timeout of 20 s against a 60 s fetch reintroduces the stampede on slow sources. From B: 1-day negative TTL for EPO 404 (A cached it for 7 days, hiding new patents), fsync before replace, IST night window, post-scrub-only demand log, transitive dataset clear, and the cashews approach for completeness.

final.chosen: Team A design (harden the two-tier cache: RequestKey with credential stripping that keeps today's hash, envelope, atomic writes, remaining-TTL promotion, in-process plus Redis single-flight sized per HTTP call, Redis re-probe, demand-driven refresh-ahead with a caller budget class, @dataset_cache registry) with Team B's negative TTL, fsync, IST night window, post-scrub demand log and transitive dataset clear
final.why_chosen: Both teams found the same root cause (no request identity, no entry envelope, no concurrency rule, no dataset ownership) and chose the same stdlib + redis-py shape. Team A's details are more correct: its canonical string is identical to today's when no key is set, so existing disk entries survive without B's one-TTL dual lookup; its Redis lock is per HTTP call with blocking_timeout longer than the fetch, whereas B's 20 s blocking_timeout is shorter than the 60 s client timeout, so waiters would give up and stampede a slow source exactly when single-flight matters; A also adds a caller dimension to _over_budget and per-layer counters. Team B contributes small, sound refinements: a shorter negative TTL, fsync, a night window and a privacy rule for the demand log.

approaches.name: Harden the existing two-tier cache: canonical request identity + envelope + atomic writes + two-level single-flight + demand-driven refresh-ahead + dataset cache registry
approaches.how: A RequestKey (source, url, params minus credential params) is the single identity for cache, lock, demand log and warming. Disk and Redis store a small envelope {v, status, fetched_at, req, body}; disk writes go to a temp file then os.replace; unreadable files are a miss and are deleted. Promotion to Redis uses the remaining TTL. A per-source cacheable-status set lets EPO 404 be cached as empty. In-process asyncio futures give single-flight without Redis; redis.asyncio Lock (token-safe, timeout from the httpx timeout) adds cross-process single-flight. get_redis re-probes after a back-off. A demand log of request keys drives refresh-ahead with a warming share of the budget. A @dataset_cache decorator records which datasets each lru_cache loader reads.
approaches.basis: Standard library (hashlib, os.replace, asyncio) and redis-py, which is already a dependency; refresh-ahead and single-flight are well-known cache patterns (Go singleflight, Caffeine refreshAfterWrite).
approaches.advantages: No new dependency, keeps decisions 0003/0010 and SYSTEM-DESIGN §4 two-tier layout, keeps the budget and 429 pause logic in the same function, fixes every flag at the root (identity + envelope).
approaches.drawbacks: Hand-written code to maintain (~200 lines); the envelope is a small on-disk format change that needs a legacy read path.

approaches.name: hishel (RFC 9111 HTTP cache transport for httpx)
approaches.how: Wrap the httpx.AsyncClient in hishel's AsyncCacheTransport with a file or Redis storage; caching decisions follow HTTP cache headers or a forced policy.
approaches.basis: Mature, popular httpx companion; file, Redis and SQLite storages.
approaches.advantages: Atomic storage and standard semantics for free; keys can exclude headers.
approaches.drawbacks: Caches below _get_json, so budget counting, the 429 pause and status-based negative caching need re-plumbing; OpenAlex/EPO send little useful cache metadata so a forced TTL policy is needed anyway; a second cache layer beside the existing one; no single-flight.

approaches.name: diskcache (SQLite-backed cache) as the disk tier
approaches.how: Replace the JSON file tier with diskcache.Cache(expire=ttl); use its memoize_stampede / Lock recipes for coordination.
approaches.basis: Mature pure-Python library, process-safe, used widely.
approaches.advantages: Atomic writes, expiry and eviction built in, process-safe locks across workers on one host.
approaches.drawbacks: New dependency and a data migration; synchronous API inside async code (needs to_thread); locks are per host only, so Redis still needed for several hosts; stores opaque blobs that operators cannot inspect as easily as JSON files.

approaches.name: aiocache with memory and Redis backends
approaches.how: Decorate the connectors with aiocache.cached using a Redis backend and a memory fallback; key builder strips credentials.
approaches.advantages: Async-native; pluggable key builders and serializers.
approaches.drawbacks: No durable disk tier (memory fallback is lost on restart, which is the offline default), so the 7-day cache disappears without Redis; rewrites the cache to fix what are mostly identity and coordination problems.

approaches.name: PostgreSQL table as the research cache (research_cache(key, status, fetched_at, body jsonb))
approaches.how: Store responses in a table with an index on key and fetched_at; use advisory locks for single-flight.
approaches.basis: SQLAlchemy 2 and Alembic are in the stack; advisory locks are a known single-flight tool.
approaches.advantages: Transactional writes, queryable demand, works across workers and hosts.
approaches.drawbacks: Blocked on the database being reachable (2.1.1) and breaks the offline baseline where only disk exists; puts high-churn cache rows in the system of record.

approaches.name: Static nightly warming from registry domain queries (the current 2.2.6 plan)
approaches.how: For each of 240 registry domains, run its research queries nightly under the daily cap.
approaches.drawbacks: The reviewer's probe shows the warmed keys do not match founder keys (different words, different params), and it spends the shared cap and re-fetches entries still valid for 7 days.

approaches.name: cashews decorators (locked / early-refresh strategies)
approaches.how: Decorate source functions with a caching decorator that has Redis/memory backends and built-in lock and early refresh.
approaches.basis: Popular asyncio cache libraries; cashews has 'locked' and 'early' (refresh-ahead) strategies.
approaches.drawbacks: No disk backend without Redis in the default free setup (cashews needs an extra dependency for disk); keys built from function arguments bring back the credential problem unless customised; another layer to learn.

not_chosen.name: hishel
not_chosen.reason: A second cache under the existing one; it bypasses the per-source budget and 429 pause and still needs a forced TTL and custom keying, so it adds a dependency without removing our code.

not_chosen.name: diskcache
not_chosen.reason: New dependency plus a migration to fix atomicity that os.replace fixes in three lines; sync API in async code; still needs Redis for cross-host locks.

not_chosen.name: aiocache
not_chosen.reason: Loses the disk tier, which is the only cache in the free offline setup.

not_chosen.name: PostgreSQL cache table
not_chosen.reason: Blocked on 2.1.1 and fails the offline baseline; cache churn does not belong in the system of record.

not_chosen.name: Static registry warming
not_chosen.reason: Proven to warm keys founders never request while spending their shared budget.

not_chosen.name: cashews decorators (locked / early-refresh strategies)
not_chosen.reason: Has single-flight and refresh-ahead built in, but no disk backend without an extra dependency in the default no-Redis setup, and argument-built keys bring back the credential problem; we would use two features of a large library.

design.components: 1) research/cache_key.py: RequestKey(source, method, url, params) with CREDENTIAL_PARAMS = {'api_key','mailto','key','token','access_token'} stripped; .digest() = sha1 of the canonical string 'GET {url} {json.dumps(params_wo_creds, sort_keys=True)}' (identical to today's string when no key is set, so today's disk entries stay valid); .redis_key() = 'rs:{source}:{digest}' (aligns 2.2.2). 2) Cache (research/sources.py) stores Envelope {v:1, status, fetched_at (epoch s), req {url, params}, body}; get() reads legacy raw files as status 200 with fetched_at = mtime; corrupt/unreadable file -> log cache.corrupt with the file name, unlink, return miss; put() writes '{name}.{pid}.{rand}.tmp' then os.replace; Redis promotion uses ex = ttl - age (skip when <= 0). 3) CACHEABLE_STATUS per source: default {200}, epo {200, 404} (404 stored as status 404 with body None; epo_patents already maps 404 to (0, [])). 4) SingleFlight: dict[digest, asyncio.Future] in-process; with Redis, an outer redis.asyncio.lock.Lock('lock:{source}:{digest}', timeout=http_timeout+10, blocking_timeout=http_timeout+15). Order: cache -> join in-process flight -> Redis lock -> re-check cache -> pause -> budget -> fetch -> store -> release. Waiters re-run the cache and pause checks after waking, never the fetch blindly. 5) core/redis.py: failure memo becomes (None, retry_at); re-probe after settings.redis_retry_s (60 s); redis_state() -> 'off' | 'up' | 'down'; counters cache_stats {redis_hit, disk_hit, miss, redis_down_reads} for 5.4.2. 6) Demand log: every founder-originated lookup (hit or miss) records its digest: Redis ZINCRBY 'rs:demand:{yyyy-mm-dd}' (TTL 8 days) or, without Redis, an append-only line in {cache_dir}/demand/{date}.log. 7) Budget caller class: _over_budget(source, caller='founder'|'warm'); warm may use at most research_warm_share (0.25) of the per-source cap (T15 owns the per-source cap table) and, when no cap is set, at most research_warm_max per source per night. 8) scripts/warm_research_cache.py (nightly, 5.4.4): digests demanded >= 2 times in the last 7 days whose envelope expires within 36 h, replayed from envelope.req with caller='warm', most-demanded first, stopping at the warm budget; it never refetches a fresh entry. 9) core/datasets.py: @dataset_cache('banking', 'ecosystem') wraps functools.lru_cache and registers fn -> datasets; clear(dataset) clears every loader that declared it; version(dataset) = sha1 of the data files' (size, mtime) for 2.2.3 and the 2.2.4 ETag. Merged from Team B: fsync before os.replace; negative TTL research_negative_days (1) for EPO 404; warmer limited to a 22:00-05:00 IST window; demand log keeps only post-scrub params; dataset clear is transitive.
design.data_model: Envelope JSON {"v":1,"status":200|404,"fetched_at":1760000000,"req":{"url":...,"params":{...without credentials}},"body":...}. Redis keys: rs:{source}:{digest} (EX remaining ttl), lock:{source}:{digest}, rs:neg:{source} (pause, unchanged meaning), rs:demand:{date} (ZSET digest->count), budget:{source}:{date}:{caller}. DATASETS registry: dict[str, set[Callable]] plus DATA_FILES: dict[str, list[Path]]. Envelope ttl is chosen by status: 200 -> research_cache_days, 404 -> research_negative_days.
design.algorithm: lookup(req, caller): k=RequestKey(req); env=cache.get(k) -> if env and fresh: record_demand(k) if caller=='founder'; return env. fut=flights.get(k): if fut: return await fut. Create fut; try: async with redis_lock(k) (or nullcontext): env=cache.get(k); if env: resolve; if paused(source): resolve 429; if over_budget(source, caller): resolve 429; r=await http; if r.status in CACHEABLE_STATUS[source]: cache.put(k, Envelope(...)); if 429: pause(); resolve (status, body) finally: flights.pop(k). Remaining TTL on promotion: ttl - (now - fetched_at).
design.interfaces: T15 (A3) owns per-source limits and the per-source status vocabulary; T08 adds the caller dimension and the RequestKey that T15's counters use. T13 relies on SourceResult statuses staying honest (a cached 404 is 'ok, 0 found', a budget refusal is 'budget_exhausted'). T33 eval fixtures can be recorded as envelopes (req + status + body) and replayed, including degraded statuses. T23 reads cache_stats and redis_state. 2.2.3 (version key) and 2.2.4 (ETags) call datasets.clear/version. T32's maintenance runner calls Cache.purge() and the warmer.
files: backend/app/ecosystem/index.py and the ~25 lru_cache loaders (decorator swap)
design.rollout: Step 1 (no behaviour risk): RequestKey + envelope with legacy read + atomic write + remaining TTL + EPO 404; existing disk entries remain valid because the canonical string equals today's when no key is set. Step 2: single-flight (in-process first, Redis lock second) and the Redis re-probe. Step 3: dataset registry (mechanical decorator swap, one PR per package). Step 4: demand log, then the warmer once 2.2.6's key is in place. Old Redis rs:{hash} keys simply expire within 7 days.
design.offline: Without Redis everything still works: disk tier with atomic envelopes, in-process single-flight, in-process budget counters, a local demand log; the warmer reads the local logs. Without network, cached envelopes still answer and misses report 'error' or 'budget_exhausted' honestly.

approaches.name: Directory-only supply map with a three-valued gap and cited reference files
approaches.how: Matches are the MCA makers from suppliers_for. Gap is a Tri verdict: covered (makers found), gap (the directory has no maker for the category), or outside coverage (the founder's district is not in the directory: UNKNOWN). Cluster pointers and district centroids are Git-held, cited JSON files in the backend; the frontend renders what the API returns.
approaches.basis: suppliers_for already returns real companies; reference data in Git is the repo rule (SYSTEM-DESIGN 2, 5.3); SM1 and SM6.
approaches.advantages: Only real data reaches founders; one gap definition for /supply, /suppliers and 4.2.2; honest about coverage.
approaches.drawbacks: No price or capacity columns until the founder adds quotes; the centroid and cluster files need curation.

approaches.name: Lexicographic CP-SAT (two or three solves)
approaches.how: Solve 1 maximises placed units, and that optimum is fixed as a constraint. Solve 2 minimises landed cost (price plus founder-entered delivery), and that optimum is fixed too. Solve 3 maximises local and trusted choices as a tie-breaker among cost-optimal plans.
approaches.basis: The standard lexicographic (pre-emptive) multi-objective method; OR-Tools CP-SAT is already in the stack; the models are tiny (20 lines x 100 quotes).
approaches.advantages: Correct for any price scale with no magic constants; every preference is explainable, in order.
approaches.drawbacks: Two to three solves (milliseconds each at this size).

approaches.name: Single weighted objective with a data-derived big-M and percentage penalties
approaches.how: Penalty per short unit = (max unit price + max penalties) * 100 + 1; distance and trust as a percentage of the unit price.
approaches.basis: Common big-M practice in MIP modelling.
approaches.drawbacks: Large coefficients at 10^7 units risk overflow or slow search; the percentages are invented tuning numbers presented as 'rules'.

approaches.name: Keep seed matching with an 'example' label; add quote-fed scoring later
approaches.how: Label invented suppliers as examples; when the founder's quotes move server-side (3.1.3), score them with the 40/30/20/10 scorer.
approaches.drawbacks: Invented companies and prices stay in front of founders, the gap stays meaningless, and the owner's D9 preference is 'not fetched' over labelled demos.

approaches.name: PostGIS spatial index over the full MCA file
approaches.how: Load all 78,689 companies into PostgreSQL with geometry and query by distance.
approaches.basis: PostGIS is the standard spatial extension.
approaches.advantages: Scales and ranks by true distance.
approaches.drawbacks: Reference data lives in Git by design, the database is not live yet (2.1.1), and haversine over a few thousand rows in Python is already fast enough.

approaches.drawbacks: Violates the free/offline constraint; India Post PIN centroids give enough precision for 'nearest' at district scale.

approaches.drawbacks: Nominatim's usage policy forbids bulk geocoding (1 request/s, ~78k addresses, truncated addresses); a separate data job with its own quality problems.

design.algorithm: Gap: if the founder's district is not in the directory's districts -> outside_coverage (UNKNOWN) with 'our directory covers Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai today'. Stage 2 minimises sum((price + delivery) * 100 * x) in paise and adds cost == best2. Stage 3 maximises sum(local[s] * x) + sum(trusted[s] * y) as a tie-breaker. why_unmet comes from the stage-1 model: capacity, MOQ, budget, or 'no supplier with known prices'. 'Capacity taken by your other lines' is said only when another line actually uses that supplier. MOQ alternative: for each unmet line and each same-category supplier whose min_order is above the need and whose remaining capacity after the solve is at least min_order, offer 'buy min_order: extra units, extra cost', cheapest first.

approaches.name: Shared rule-based utterance reader: boundary-aware cue sets, a NegEx-style negation window, a correction grammar, positional place resolution and a cited town gazetteer
approaches.how: One module tokenises with character spans; CueSets compile word-boundary regexes (explicit stem* marker for prefixes like manufactur*); each hit carries span and a negated flag from a short trigger window (no, not, never, without, n't, illai, yet-to) closed by scope breakers (but, comma, however, actually); a correction parser recognises 'X not Y', 'not Y, X', 'actually X', 'instead of Y', 'change Y to X'; place mentions are resolved by polarity, role cue (in/from/based vs sell to/market) and position; a town->district gazetteer from the India Post directory adds towns.
approaches.basis: NegEx (Chapman et al. 2001) is the standard rule approach to negation scope, widely used in clinical NLP; word-boundary regex and gazetteers are the established baseline for slot filling; India Post data is already cited in the repo.
approaches.advantages: Offline, deterministic, explainable, works on Tanglish with a few Tamil triggers, testable against the eval set; fits decision 0002 (code decides).
approaches.drawbacks: Rules need curation and a negative-case corpus; free word order and unusual phrasing will still be missed and must fall back to a question.

approaches.name: spaCy with PhraseMatcher, EntityRuler and negspacy
approaches.how: Tokenise and match cues and places with spaCy pipelines; negspacy marks negated entities.
approaches.basis: Mature, popular NLP library; negspacy implements NegEx.
approaches.advantages: Robust tokenisation, lemmas, ready negation component.
approaches.drawbacks: Adds a large dependency and a model download (en_core_web_sm), English-only (Tamil/Tanglish replies), and the negation and correction logic still has to be written for our slots.

approaches.name: Model-based structured extraction (Gemini free tier / Ollama) with a JSON schema
approaches.how: Ask the model for {slot: value, negated, corrected_from} per reply; validate in code.
approaches.advantages: Handles free phrasing and Tamil well when available.
approaches.drawbacks: Absent offline and on quota exhaustion, slow on CPU Ollama, and decision 0002 says code decides gates such as confirmation; may be added later only as a proposer ranked below founder answers via T03.

approaches.name: Fuzzy matching (rapidfuzz) for places and cues
approaches.how: Score tokens against gazetteer and cue lists with edit distance thresholds.
approaches.drawbacks: Raises false positives, the very problem being fixed; does not address negation or correction. Kept as a possible later add-on for towns only.

approaches.how: Train an intent model on labelled confirmation replies.
approaches.drawbacks: No labelled data exists; new dependency; still needs span-level parsing to know what was corrected.

design.components: 1) elicitation/reader.py: tokens(text) -> list[Tok(text, low, start, end, i)]; CueSet(mapping value->cues) compiled to one alternation regex with (?<!\w) / (?!\w) boundaries, 'stem*' for prefixes, optional plural s; find(text) -> list[Mention(value, cue, start, end, negated)] ordered by position. 2) Negation: PRE triggers {no, not, never, without, none, nothing, nobody, don't, doesn't, didn't, haven't, hasn't, isn't, aren't, wasn't, can't, won't, yet to, illai, illa, alla}; window = up to 4 tokens after the trigger, closed by breakers {but, however, though, actually, instead, ',', ';', '.'}; pseudo-negations {not only, no doubt, not just} ignored; POST triggers {not yet} within 2 tokens after a mention. 3) places.py: find_places(text) -> list[PlaceMention(district, candidates, name, start, end, negated, role, via)]; role = 'home' after {in, at, from, based in, live in, unit in, near} | 'market' after {sell in, sell to, market in, supply to, customers in} | None; via in {district, alias, town}. resolve_district(mentions, corrected_span=None): drop negated; prefer a mention inside a correction's new-value span; then role home; then first by position; role market never fills district. 4) elicitation/data/tn_towns.json: {town: district | [districts]} from the India Post all-India pincode directory (data.gov.in, the source already used by scripts/build_ecosystem.py), S.O/H.O office names with suffixes stripped, generic names removed via a reviewed exclusion list; built by scripts/build_town_gazetteer.py with _meta {source, retrieved, rows, ambiguous}. Ambiguous towns return candidates, never a guess. 5) elicitation/corrections.py: parse_corrections(text, filled_slots) -> list[Correction(slot, new_value|None, rejected_value|None, span)]; patterns per slot type use the reader: places, sector/form CueSets, stage cues, money. 'not Y' alone -> rejected Y, new None. 6) elicitation/confirmation.py: read_reply(text) -> Verdict in {AFFIRM, REJECT, AFFIRM_WITH_CHANGES, UNCLEAR} using negation-aware YES/NO cue sets ('not right', 'not correct' -> REJECT) plus corrections. 7) engine.confirm(session, verdict, corrections): AFFIRM and no corrections -> generate; any correction -> apply as founder corrections (T03 source 'correction', locked), stay CONFIRMING and restate the changed objective ('Got it, Salem. So: ...'); REJECT without corrections -> Action(kind='ask_which', options=[restated facts]) rendered as a question by voice and as chips on screen; UNCLEAR -> repeat the restatement once, then ask_which. 8) extract.py: all cue lists become CueSets compiled from T01's canonical vocabulary; negated sector/form/stage mentions are not emitted (negated stage mentions are returned as excluded values for the selector); positional 'problem' guess flagged positional=True. 9) engine.observe: run parse_corrections first in every state, apply them as corrections; skip positional extractions when answering a slot other than problem; session.put rule (with T03): a positional guess never replaces an existing value. 10) answers._stage: CueSet + negation; negated revenue/growth cues never return revenue; if only negated cues match, return None so the question is re-asked with the remaining options. Merged from Team B: positional guess emitted only for free descriptions or the problem slot, 'not wrong' reads as yes, Taluk names in the gazetteer, ask_which outside the question budget.
design.data_model: Mention(value, cue, start, end, negated: bool). PlaceMention(district: str|None, candidates: list[str], name, start, end, negated, role, via). Correction(slot: str, new_value: Any|None, rejected_value: Any|None, span: tuple[int,int]). Verdict enum. Action gains kind 'ask_which' with options: list[{slot, label, value}]. tn_towns.json {"_meta": {...}, "towns": {"pollachi": "coimbatore", "kumbakonam": "thanjavur", "<ambiguous>": ["a","b"]}}.
design.algorithm: Negation: for each mention m, look back over tokens before m.start until a breaker or 4 tokens; negated if a PRE trigger is found and it is not part of a pseudo-negation; also negated if a POST trigger follows within 2 tokens. Correction grammar (applied on spans): 'A not B' / 'A, not B' -> new A, rejected B (same slot type); 'not B, (it is|its|but) A' -> same; 'actually|sorry|I mean A' -> new A; 'instead of B' -> rejected B; 'change B to A' -> new A, rejected B. Confirmation: REJECT if a NO cue is un-negated or a YES cue is negated; AFFIRM if an un-negated YES cue and no NO cue; corrections present -> AFFIRM_WITH_CHANGES (or REJECT with corrections, handled the same way). District resolution order: correction span > home role > first by position; negated and market-role mentions never fill district.
design.interfaces: T01: cue lists and slot enums come from the canonical vocabulary module; T10 owns only the matcher. T03: corrections are written through T03's typed put with a 'correction' source that outranks extraction and locks the slot (1.1.2.3). T05/T27: 'ask_which' is a typed pending action in T27's state machine and does not count against T05's question budget (repair, not elicitation). T09: b2b decompose uses CueSet. T13: scrub reuses the town gazetteer. T33: eval adds the trap corpus and replays (Pollachi, 'not right', 'Salem not Madurai', beneficiary answer) as assertions.
design.rollout: PR 1: positional problem guard (small, independent). PR 2: reader + CueSet swap in extract/answers (behaviour change limited to removed false positives; run the eval). PR 3: negation in stage and cues. PR 4: places positional + gazetteer data PR. PR 5: corrections + confirmation verdict + engine.confirm signature + _advance. Each PR runs the eval set and the trap corpus.
design.offline: Entirely offline: standard library regex and a committed JSON gazetteer. Nothing depends on a model; an optional model proposer (later) would only add candidate values below founder answers.

approaches.name: Session lifecycle registry in process: explicit job outcomes with failure notices and backoff, per-kind concurrency limits, tombstones on delete, ref-counted turn locks acquired inside the stream, and an idle sweep tied to the store's expiry; durable rows later cascade from agent_sessions (Team B called it the session lifecycle service with end_session as the single delete path)
approaches.how: One module owns per-session in-process state and applies the session idle expiry from T07's store contract. Jobs carry attempts and a terminal outcome; wait returns the outcome; failures notify listeners and back off; semaphores bound concurrent jobs; delete writes a tombstone that start/put refuse, cancels jobs and waits for the turn lock; locks exist only while held or awaited; a sweep (lifespan task plus opportunistic call on create) removes idle rows, finished jobs, empty listener sets and expired MemoryStore documents.
approaches.basis: Plain asyncio primitives (Task, Semaphore, Lock) and the existing Board interface; ref-counted keyed locks are a standard keyed-mutex pattern; tombstones are the standard guard against write-after-delete.
approaches.advantages: No dependency, works in the offline single-process baseline today, keeps decision 0010's job board, and the same contract (outcome states, tombstone, cascade) carries over to 2.3.1's Redis queue and table.
approaches.drawbacks: Per-process only (correct, because the state is per process), and one more small module to maintain.

design.components: 1) agents/lifecycle.py (new): SessionLocks with acquire(session_id, timeout=None) as an async context manager over dict[str, (Lock, waiters)]; the entry is created on first acquire and removed when the holder releases with zero waiters, so the map holds only active sessions. Tombstones: dict[str, expires_at] with TTL = T07 idle expiry; is_forgotten(id). touch(id) records last activity. sweep(now) removes everything idle beyond the expiry. 2) agents/jobs.py: Outcome = Literal['done','running','failed','none']; Job gains attempts, finished_at, reason ('timeout', 'source_error', 'budget', from T15 when available) and retry_at; wait() returns Outcome; start() refuses a session that is_forgotten, returns the failed job instead of restarting it until retry_at (backoff 30 s, 2 min, 10 min; max 3 attempts per idea version, reset when the idea version changes, T06); run() re-checks is_forgotten before results.put and notify; per-kind asyncio.Semaphore (settings.job_concurrency_research=4, council=2) taken inside run(); notify_failure sends {'kind','state':'failed','reason','retry_at'}. 3) agents/results.py: MemoryResults rows store (written_at, touched_at, payload); get/latest update touched_at; sweep(cutoff) drops rows untouched since cutoff; latest() uses a per-session index instead of scanning every row. 4) agents/store.py MemoryStore: get() pops an expired document; sweep() pops all expired documents. 5) routers/ideation.py: agent_turn and agent_turn_stream use lifecycle locks; the stream route does a lock-free _load (404 for unknown ids, no lock entry created), then acquires the lock inside the generator and reloads; agent_delete: tombstone -> board.forget (cancel jobs, drop results, close listeners) -> acquire the turn lock with a timeout (5 s) -> store.delete; the notices stream emits a 'failed' SSE event. 6) ideation.py: _search/_convene/offline paths branch on Outcome; 'failed' is narrated once per attempt from a template ('I could not search this time: <reason>. I will try again in a few minutes, or ask me to retry.'), recorded in s.narrated; never 'still searching' for a failed job. 7) main.py lifespan: start an asyncio task calling lifecycle.sweep every settings.sweep_interval_s (600 s) and cancel it on shutdown; agent_start also calls sweep opportunistically every 100 creates (covers tests and servers without lifespan). 8) 2.3.1 spec: agent_results(session_id FK -> agent_sessions ON DELETE CASCADE, idea_version, kind, payload, written_at); 3.2.4 retention and erasure lists name results. Merged from Team B: lifecycle.end_session(id) as the single delete entry point (used by DELETE, T07 expiry and T32), an apply_erasures hook called by the sweep, a MemoryStore LRU cap, and failure sentences in the phrasebook.
design.data_model: Job {session_id, kind, task, started, attempts, finished_at, outcome, reason, retry_at}. MemoryResults row {(session, version, kind): (written_at, touched_at, payload_json)}. Tombstones {session_id: expires_at}. Lock map {session_id: (asyncio.Lock, waiters:int)}. Notice event 'failed' {kind, reason, retry_at}.
design.algorithm: Delete: tombstone(id); await board.forget(id) (cancel, drop, close); try: async with locks.acquire(id, timeout=5): await store.delete(id) except timeout: await store.delete(id) (the running turn's save then fails its version check and is discarded). Start: if forgotten -> None; current failed and now < retry_at -> return current; else new task. Sweep: cutoff = now - idle_expiry; drop finished jobs with finished_at < cutoff, results with touched_at < cutoff, listener entries with empty sets, tombstones past expiry, MemoryStore documents expired; running jobs are never removed.
design.interfaces: T07 provides IDLE_EXPIRY and the store contract (expiry vs retention); lifecycle reads it rather than redefining 6 hours. T06 provides the idea version used to reset retry attempts. T28 adds the 'failed' event to the typed SSE union and the client queue; the Talk screen resolves tool chips on it. T23 exposes gauges (jobs, results rows, locks, tombstones). final.tests: Unit: a job raising TimeoutError -> wait returns 'failed', one 'failed' notice, four turns later the work ran once (then again only after retry_at); narration says 'could not search' once and never SEARCHING. Locks: 1,000 turns on distinct ids leave an empty lock map; a stream response whose body is never iterated leaves the lock free; random unknown ids do not create entries. Delete race: start a turn that blocks inside a tool, DELETE, then let the turn continue -> no results row and no job for the id, and the turn's save is refused. Sweep: with a fake clock, 1,000 sessions idle 7 h -> zero jobs, results, MemoryStore docs and listeners after one sweep; a running job is never removed. Concurrency: 10 research starts -> at most 4 running work functions at once. Added: 2001 MemoryStore sessions -> the least recently active is evicted and logged; T07 expiry and DELETE both go through end_session.
final.risks: A sweep that removes a result a resumed session still needs: touched_at is refreshed on every read and on every turn (touch), and the cutoff equals the session idle expiry, so a live session's rows are never older. The delete timeout path relies on the store's version check rejecting the late save (MemoryStore and SqlStore both do). Semaphores add queueing latency under bursts; the turn already waits only briefly and narrates 'still searching' only for genuinely running jobs. The memory cap evicts the oldest conversation on a busy offline server; it is logged and the founder sees the existing not-saved notice.

verdicts.reasoning: Both diagnoses are right (scan._local swallows exceptions; _statement's crowded fallback with no counted pair; registry summary words in public_vocabulary; denylist scrub; two matchers). A's plan is slightly more detailed and contributes the single_part and crowded_parts_only wording, place removal in scrub, _meta-driven districts/size in cohort/reference.py and the session-aware Cohort page.

final.chosen: Team B design (evidence ledger with a declarative CLAIMS table of preconditions for every statement and lever, LocalResult with status and scope, one IDF-anchored stdlib matcher cached via T08's dataset registry, document-frequency filler removal and allowlist-only scrub with an OpenAlex topic snapshot) with Team A's specific single-part/uncounted-combination templates, place-aware scrub, _meta-driven corpus scope and session-aware Cohort page
final.why_chosen: Both teams traced the false claims to wording chosen without a record of what was searched, and both built a LocalResult, a single matcher and an allowlist scrub. B's claims table makes the honesty rule structural (each template declares its precondition over the ledger and falls through in order) and is stricter where it matters: 'crowded' requires no failed pair, not just one counted pair. It also reuses T08's dataset registry. A contributes more informative fallback wording than a bare 'unclear', drops places from model-written terms, and removes the hard-coded three districts and 654 count.

design.algorithm: Statement order: combination gap (needs >= 1 pair with status ok and gap) -> context gap (needs context ok AND local ok; text '...and among the {records} startups the TN Startup Map lists for {districts}, I found none doing it') -> rarest element -> crowded (needs pairs_counted >= 1, pairs_failed == 0 and every part ok) -> unclear ('I could check only {k} of the parts; the combination was not counted'). Single-part ideas never reach 'crowded'; they get 'element' or 'unclear'. The localise lever needs local.status == ok and repeats the scoped wording. Matching: score = sum of idf of shared stems; accept when |shared - FILLER| >= 2 and max idf(shared) >= ANCHOR_IDF; the cohort count shown is the number accepted.

verdicts.reasoning: Diagnoses identical and correct (config.secret_key 'change-me' with is_production unused; refresh jti never stored; authenticate_user short-circuits bcrypt; RateLimitMiddleware keys on request.state.user_id which nothing sets). A keeps register's 409, so F-A3-010's status-code enumeration stays at full speed behind only a rate limit; B returns a generic reply and documents the residual. B's principal middleware and counters are shared mechanisms reused by T17/T19 and research budgets, and it delegates trusted-proxy handling to uvicorn's ProxyHeadersMiddleware. A's 30 s grace for concurrent-tab refresh is a real correctness gap in B (two tabs would revoke a founder's family), so it is merged with A's purge, startup-refresh and limit_class details.

final.chosen: Team B design (settings guard with SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS verification window, constant-time login and generic registration reply, SM5 principal middleware shared with T17/T19, counters.hit with Redis INCR+EXPIRE and bounded memory fallback reused by research budgets, route cost classes with IP backstop and uvicorn's ProxyHeadersMiddleware for trusted proxies, durable rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, logout and a single-flight client refresh) with Team A's concurrent-tab grace, expired-row purge, startup refresh, limit_class and rollover pruning
final.why_chosen: Both teams found the same two-part root cause (no principal, no durable token state) and the same fixes. B is wiser on fit and on the enumeration flag: its principal and counters are shared mechanisms (SM5) that T17, T19 and the research source budgets reuse, it uses uvicorn's existing ProxyHeadersMiddleware instead of hand-parsing X-Forwarded-For, it also guards other dev defaults in production, and it closes the register status-code channel instead of keeping the 409 as A does. A adds the 30 s grace that prevents false theft detection from two tabs, which B lacks, plus a few operational details.

approaches.name: Principal middleware plus Redis-or-memory window counters with route cost classes (in-house)
approaches.how: One middleware resolves the principal: the verified bearer sub (no DB hit), else the session id in agent/voice paths, else the client IP, honouring only trusted proxies. Limits are per class (turn, speak, notices-connect, auth, default) and per principal, counted in Redis INCR+EXPIRE fixed windows with a bounded in-process dict as fallback. An IP backstop cap applies to session and anonymous principals.
approaches.basis: The same INCR+EXPIRE pattern as research/sources.py _over_budget; Redis rate limits are in SYSTEM-DESIGN 4.1 L1; the Starlette middleware is already in place.
approaches.advantages: Fair under CGNAT, shared across workers, memory bounded by TTL, no new dependency, and testable through the in-memory fallback without a Redis server.
approaches.drawbacks: Fixed windows allow a burst at a window edge (acceptable at these limits), and we own a little code.

approaches.name: slowapi / limits library
approaches.how: Decorate routes with per-route limits, with Redis or memory storage and a key function that returns the principal.
approaches.basis: A popular port of Flask-Limiter for Starlette/FastAPI; limits supports moving windows.
approaches.advantages: Moving windows and per-route rules are prebuilt.
approaches.drawbacks: A new dependency and decorator changes across routers; the keying decision (the principal) still has to be written; its key format differs from SYSTEM-DESIGN's Redis key table.

approaches.name: Reverse-proxy limiting (nginx limit_req / Caddy rate_limit)
approaches.how: Limit at the proxy by IP or header.
approaches.drawbacks: Hosting is undecided; the proxy cannot see the JWT subject or session cheaply; not testable in the repo or in local runs.

approaches.name: DB-backed rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, plus a single-flight refresh in the client
approaches.how: A refresh_tokens table (hashed jti, family_id, user_id, expires_at, revoked_at, replaced_by). /refresh rotates and revokes the presented token; presenting a revoked token revokes its whole family; /logout revokes. api.ts retries once on 401 after one shared refresh call.
approaches.basis: Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection from the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP; SQLAlchemy/Alembic are already used.
approaches.advantages: Durable revocation without Redis; logout works server-side; theft is detected; fits erasure (delete by user).
approaches.drawbacks: One DB write per refresh (every 30 minutes per active user: negligible).

approaches.basis: fastapi-users is popular; hosted IdPs (Auth0, Clerk) are mature.
approaches.drawbacks: Replaces the working User model and services (a large migration); hosted IdPs break free/offline and send founder identities to a third party.
approaches.cost: free/open source (fastapi-users); paid beyond free tiers and online (hosted IdPs)

approaches.drawbacks: No second verifier service exists, so it is key-management overhead for no gain now.

approaches.drawbacks: Redis is optional, so revocation silently disappears when it is off; no reuse detection; nothing to delete with the user under 3.2.4.

design.components: 1) core/config.py: a model_validator(mode='after') that refuses a secret_key in a denylist ('change-me', '', 'secret') or shorter than 32 bytes when app_env != 'development'. An optional secret_key_previous. In production the same guard reports the other dev defaults (postgres password, MinIO keys) as errors. 2) core/security.py: decode_token tries secret_key, then secret_key_previous; tokens carry a kid fingerprint for logging. 3) models/refresh_token.py + migration: refresh_tokens(id, user_id FK, jti_hash sha256, family_id, issued_at, expires_at, revoked_at, replaced_by). 4) services/auth_service.py: issuing stores the refresh jti; refresh rotates (revokes the old token and issues a new one in the same family); reuse of a revoked jti revokes the family and returns 401 TOKEN_REUSED; logout revokes the family. authenticate_user verifies against a module-level dummy bcrypt hash when the user is missing. On a duplicate, register returns the same 202 and message as a fresh registration ('If this email is new, the account is ready; sign in'). 5) routers/auth.py: POST /logout. 6) core/identity.py IdentityMiddleware (SM5) sets the principal: the bearer token, decoded without a DB hit (an invalid token means anonymous, and the route still rejects it); else the session id parsed from /api/v1/ideation/agent/sessions/{id}/...; else the IP. Trusted proxies come from settings.forwarded_allow_ips via uvicorn's ProxyHeadersMiddleware. 7) core/counters.py: hit(key, window_s, limit) -> (allowed, remaining, reset), using a Redis INCR+EXPIRE pipeline, else an in-process dict pruned on access and capped (oldest windows evicted). 8) core/middleware.py: RateLimitMiddleware rewritten around route classes. 9) Frontend: api.ts does a single-flight refresh on 401, then one retry; auth.tsx logs out via /logout; agentClient.ts listenNotices reconnects with backoff on error and resumes notices. Merged from Team A: 30 s concurrent-tab grace in reuse detection, T32 purge of expired refresh rows, startup refresh in auth.tsx, limit_class in 429 bodies, window-rollover pruning and explicit notices back-off steps.
design.data_model: Principal{kind: user|session|ip, id, ip}. Route classes in settings: turn (stream POST: 30/min per principal); speak (voice/speak: 120/min per session); notices (EventSource connect: 10/min per session; the open stream is not counted again); auth (login/register/refresh: 10/min per IP and 5/min per email hash); default (100/min per principal). ip_backstop: 600/min for session and anonymous principals. The per-worker global guard is kept. Redis keys rl:{class}:{kind}:{id}:{window_start} with TTL = window. refresh_tokens as above.
design.algorithm: Per request: classify the route, resolve the principal, then call counters.hit for the principal's limit and, for session/ip principals, the IP backstop. A refusal returns 429 with Retry-After = seconds to the window reset, and logs a structured rate_limited{class, kind} event so 5.4.1 sees rejected turns. Refresh rotation: look up jti_hash; missing or expired -> 401; revoked -> revoke the family and return 401 TOKEN_REUSED; otherwise revoke it and issue a new pair in the same family, in one transaction. Client: concurrent 401s share one in-flight refresh promise; if the refresh fails, the tokens are cleared.
design.interfaces: The SM5 principal is used by T19 (consent subject: user or session) and T17 (owner checks on session routes). counters.hit is reused by the research source budgets (theme of F-B5-001). Erasure (3.2.4) deletes refresh_tokens by user. Claiming a session (3.1.1) changes the principal from session to user; the keys are separate, so limits are not reset unfairly. T32 maintenance runner purges expired refresh_tokens rows; T23 receives rate_limited and auth.refresh_reuse events.
design.rollout: 1) The settings guard and constant-time login (no DB needed; TASKS 3.1.4). 2) The principal middleware and counters, with limits read from settings so they can be tuned without code. 3) The refresh table, rotation, logout and the client wrapper together, once the users table is live (3.1.1/2.1.1). The runbook is updated in the same PR as SECRET_KEY_PREVIOUS.
design.offline: No network calls. Redis is optional (bounded memory fallback; the health endpoint notes that limits are then per worker). PostgreSQL is needed only for sign-in, which already needs it.

tasks.title: Refuse default secrets outside development and support rotation
tasks.why: A deployment without SECRET_KEY accepts tokens anyone can forge, and rotating the key logs everyone out with no plan.
tasks.how: A Pydantic model_validator on Settings that rejects a denylisted or short secret_key when app_env != development. An optional secret_key_previous is accepted for verification only. Runbook: set PREVIOUS to the old key and KEY to the new one, wait refresh_token_expire_days, then remove PREVIOUS.
tasks.when: Now; no dependencies (TASKS 3.1.4).
tasks.what_for: Tokens cannot be forged, and the key can be rotated without a mass logout.

subtasks.text: Settings validator, and a test that Settings(app_env='production') without SECRET_KEY raises at startup.
decode_token tries the current key, then the previous one; rotate-key.md gains SECRET_KEY, with the rotation steps and their effect on sessions.

tasks.title: Constant-time login and non-revealing registration
tasks.why: Unknown emails return without the bcrypt cost and register answers 409, so anyone can test whether a person is a Vanigam founder.
tasks.how: Verify against a precomputed dummy bcrypt hash when the user is missing. On a duplicate email, register returns the same 202 shape and message as a fresh registration (no tokens), and the client signs in next. The auth route class limits per IP and per email hash (task 3) slow bulk probing. The residual register-then-login leak is documented until email verification exists.
tasks.when: Now; the rate-limit part lands with task 3.
tasks.what_for: Membership in the programme cannot be discovered from timing or status codes.

subtasks.text: Dummy-hash verification with a timing test (unknown vs known email within a tolerance); a generic register reply.

tasks.title: Principal middleware and shared window counters with route classes
tasks.why: The limiter never sees the user or session, keys everyone behind one carrier IP together, grows without bound and is per process. TTS and notices calls trigger 429s that silently stop evidence updates.
tasks.how: IdentityMiddleware sets request.state.principal: the bearer sub decoded without a DB hit, else the session id from the path, else the trusted-proxy client IP. RateLimitMiddleware classifies routes (turn, speak, notices, auth, default) and calls counters.hit per principal plus an IP backstop. Redis INCR+EXPIRE when available, otherwise a bounded, pruned dict. Rejected requests are logged with their class and principal kind. 429 bodies carry a limit_class field so the client can tell a speak limit from a turn limit (from Team A); the notices reconnect back-off is 2 s, 5 s, 15 s, capped at 60 s (from Team A); the in-memory fallback drops all keys of older windows at rollover in addition to its cap (from Team A).
tasks.when: After task 1. Provides SM5 to T19 task 4 and to T17's owner checks.
tasks.what_for: Founders on one network do not lock each other out, limits hold across workers, and memory stays bounded.

subtasks.text: IdentityMiddleware decodes the bearer token and sets request.state.principal (the user id for signed-in callers).
Session-keyed buckets for agent and voice routes, separate classes for speak and notices, and an IP backstop cap.
counters.hit with Redis INCR+EXPIRE and a bounded in-memory fallback; trusted-proxy handling via forwarded_allow_ips; a test that 10,000 distinct IPs leave the fallback dict at its cap.
Log rate_limited{class, principal_kind}; in agentClient.ts the notices EventSource reconnects with backoff on error.

tasks.title: Durable rotating refresh tokens, logout and client refresh
tasks.why: Founders are signed out every 30 minutes, a stolen refresh token stays valid for 14 days, and sign-out on a shared phone does not end the server session.
tasks.where: backend/app/models/refresh_token.py (new), migration 0005_refresh_tokens, backend/app/services/auth_service.py, backend/app/routers/auth.py (/logout), frontend/src/api.ts, frontend/src/auth.tsx
tasks.how: Store the hashed jti with its family. Rotate on refresh; reuse revokes the family; /logout revokes. api.ts wraps fetch with one shared refresh on 401 and a single retry. auth.tsx calls /logout and clears browser state (3.1.5.1). A revoked token presented within 30 s of its replacement being issued is treated as a concurrent-tab race (return 401 without revoking the family) rather than theft (from Team A). Expired rows are purged by T32's maintenance runner (from Team A). On app startup, auth.tsx tries a refresh when /me answers TOKEN_EXPIRED instead of dropping tokens (from Team A).
tasks.when: When the users table is live (3.1.1 / 2.1.1); after task 1.
tasks.what_for: Founders stay signed in while active, and sign-out and response to theft work on the server.

subtasks.text: refresh_tokens table and migration; rotation with reuse detection; /logout; tests for rotation, reuse (family revoked) and logout. 30 s grace for concurrent tabs; T32 runner purges expired rows.
Single-flight refresh wrapper in api.ts and the logout call in auth.tsx. auth.tsx refreshes on startup TOKEN_EXPIRED instead of clearing tokens.

final.tests: Settings guard tests per environment. A token forged with 'change-me' is rejected under production settings. Previous-key verification works, and stops when the key is removed. A login timing test. A duplicate register is indistinguishable by status and body. Rate limits: two sessions behind one IP each get their own turn budget; the IP backstop still trips on a flood; speak calls do not consume the turn budget; a 429 carries Retry-After; the Redis-off fallback stays bounded; two app instances sharing a fake Redis enforce one limit. Refresh rotation, reuse and logout. The client wrapper is unit-tested with a mocked fetch (two concurrent 401s cause one refresh). Added: two tabs refreshing within 30 s do not revoke the family; replay after 30 s does; startup with an expired access token refreshes instead of signing out; 429 body names the limit class; memory counters return to zero after two idle windows.
final.risks: Session-keyed limits can be dodged by minting sessions: session creation sits in the auth/default class per IP, and the IP backstop remains. A mis-set forwarded_allow_ips would let clients spoof IPs: the default is none (direct connections only), and the health endpoint reports it. Fixed windows allow edge bursts of up to twice the limit, which is acceptable at these values. The register leak remains until email verification exists (documented). The 30 s grace lets a thief who races the owner within 30 s avoid detection once; accepted for multi-tab usability.
